props.title: Into the Night
props.initialSlug: Exec's wild LA night with mystery woman turns deadly

sections.content: Into the Night (1985) stands as a fascinating entry in the neo-noir thriller genre, blending dark comedy with genuine suspense in ways that influenced later LA-set nighttime adventures like Collateral (2004) and Nightcrawler (2014). Director John Landis, fresh off Trading Places (1983), crafts a surreal nocturnal odyssey through Los Angeles that feels like a spiritual predecessor to Martin Scorsese's After Hours (1985). Jeff Goldblum's depressed insomniac character getting caught up in an international smuggling plot captures that distinctly 1980s mix of yuppie ennui and criminal underground dealings.

sections.content: The film's use of Los Angeles at night creates a neon-lit dreamscape that would influence countless later films. The way Landis captures the city's empty streets, all-night diners, and strange characters established a template for nocturnal LA stories like Drive (2011) and Mulholland Drive (2001). The film's impressive roster of director cameos (including David Cronenberg, Jonathan Demme, and Jim Henson) adds a meta layer that speaks to Hollywood's interconnected nature.

Michelle Pfeiffer's performance as Diana marks a crucial turning point in her career, coming just before her breakout in Scarface (1983) and showing her ability to balance vulnerability with strength. The film's blend of genuine tension with moments of absurdist humor creates a unique tone that few films have successfully replicated, though echoes can be found in works like Lost Highway (1997) and Bringing Out the Dead (1999). sections.content: Into the Night represents a crucial evolution in the neo-noir genre, bridging the gap between classic noir and more contemporary takes. Its influence can be seen in films like Heat (1995) and L.A. Confidential (1997), which similarly use Los Angeles as both setting and character. The film's exploration of insomnia and alienation would later be echoed in works like Fight Club (1999) and Lost in Translation (2003).
